Hook: In February 2008 Warren Buffett wrote to Berkshire Hathaway's shareholders about the kind of business he most wanted to own. A truly great business, he wrote, must have an enduring moat that protects excellent returns on invested capital. The returns are the treasure inside the castle. And capitalism, he went on, guarantees that competitors will keep attacking any castle that earns them. The moat is whatever stops them.

Then he described three businesses. See's Candies, a chocolate maker from California. In 1972 Blue Chip Stamps, a company Buffett and Charlie Munger controlled, bought it for 25 million dollars, when running it took 8 million of capital and it earned under 5 million before tax. By 2007 it earned 82 million before tax, on only 40 million of capital. It sold 31 million pounds of candy that year, against 16 million in 1972: growth of two percent a year, nothing special. What was special was how little money the business needed. Its chocolates sell for cash and leave the shop within weeks, so almost nothing is tied up in debts or stock. FlightSafety, which trains pilots: a fine business, with an advantage Buffett thought durable. But every new aircraft needs new simulators, at over twelve million dollars each. From 1996 to 2007 it put in 509 million dollars more, and its profit rose by 159 million. And airlines, which he called the worst sort of business: growing fast, hungry for capital, earning little or nothing. If a farsighted capitalist had been present at Kitty Hawk, he wrote, he would have done his successors a huge favour by shooting Orville down. Put it as one number: what each extra dollar put into the business brought back every year. See's, about two dollars forty. FlightSafety, about thirty cents. Airlines, little or nothing.

The same country, the same years: one business made money almost out of nothing, one made a fair return, one devoured capital. Industry, Built. Part five: the moat. Why do some industries earn high returns for decades, while others never do?
Facts: Before any theory, the facts. Part 3 defined the measure that matters: the return on capital, a business's operating profit after tax, divided by all the money its owners and lenders have put in. If that return is above what the same money could earn elsewhere, the business is creating value. Now the facts. Each January the finance professor Aswath Damodaran publishes, for every American industry, the return its companies earned the year before on the capital invested in them, and what that capital costs. Here are 90 industries from the table he published in January 2026, for 2025, highest on the left. The white dots are each industry's cost of capital: what investors could expect elsewhere at the same risk, around 7 percent. Tobacco earns 63 percent on its capital. Home-improvement chains, soft drinks and software earn around thirty. At the other end, carmakers earn two percent, coal and consumer electronics lose money. In a good year most industries beat their cost of capital. The spread between them is the puzzle: in a market where anyone can build a factory, why doesn't money flood into tobacco until it earns seven percent like everything else?

Does it last? Damodaran has published the same table every year. Put each industry's average return from 2015 to 2019 along the bottom, and its average from 2022 to 2025 up the side. If returns were pure luck, the cloud would be round. If they never changed, every point would sit on the dashed line. It is neither. The rank correlation is 0.57: industries that earned a lot then mostly earn a lot now. The top quarter averaged thirty percent and still averages twenty-seven. The bottom quarter has crept up, from five to ten. And 15 of the 22 industries that were in the top quarter are still there. High returns fade, slowly, and some barely fade at all. Something is stopping the money from flooding in.
Fade: Chapter three. Why high returns fade.

Why should high returns fade at all? Picture an industry earning thirty percent on its capital, when the same money could earn seven percent elsewhere. Every investor who notices wants in. The first newcomer builds a plant and takes some of the customers. The second does the same. Prices fall, and with them the return. If nothing stops them, newcomers keep arriving until the return is no better than the capital could earn anywhere else. That is what economists mean by competition, and it is why, in most industries, high returns do not last. A moat bends the curve. Newcomers can still come, but they cannot reach part of what the incumbents earn, and the return settles well above the cost of capital. The facts in the last chapter look like a world with some of each: most returns drift towards the middle, slowly, and a few hardly move.

Does it happen in real industries? Take the eighty-eight industries in Damodaran's tables every year from 2015 to 2025, sort them by their return in 2015 into five groups, and follow each group's average. The top fifth started at 33 percent and ten years later earned 27. The bottom fifth started at 4 percent and climbed to 11. The groups in between drifted toward the middle. That is the pull of competition, measured: money flows toward high returns and away from low ones. But look at the top line. After ten years the best industries of 2015 still earned nearly twice what the middle did. The pull is real, and it is slow. Something is holding it back.
Value: Chapter four. Where the excess profit is.

A percentage hides how much money is at stake. Multiply each industry's return above its cost of capital by the capital it uses, and you get its profit above what that capital could have earned anywhere else. Economists call it economic profit. For American companies in 2025 it came to about 1.5 trillion dollars, against about 107 billion lost by the industries that earned less than their cost. And it is not spread evenly. Each block is an industry's share. Five industries, software: entertainment, software: systems, computers, chips and health care support, earn 39 percent of it. The castles with the deepest moats in the American economy are, overwhelmingly, the ones built from software and silicon. Notice what they share with Part 4: software costs almost nothing to copy once written, and the leading chip and computer makers sit furthest down their learning curves. The cost curve and the moat are often the same thing seen from two sides.
Variance: Is a high return the industry's doing, or the company's? Picture every business as a castle on a hill. Some hills are higher than others: that is the industry. Some castles are taller than their neighbours: that is the company. In 1997 Anita McGahan and Michael Porter measured the two. They took the profitability of the business units of American public companies, from 1981 to 1994, and asked how much of the differences between them each thing explained. The year explained 2 percent, the parent company 4. The industry explained 19 percent. The business itself, 32. And 43 percent they could not explain at all. So the hill matters: about a fifth of the differences in profit come from the industry a business is in. But the castle matters more. The rest of this part is about both: the barriers that protect a whole industry, and the advantages that protect one company from its neighbours.
Conc: The simplest thing to measure about an industry's castles is how many there are, and how much of the land the biggest ones hold. Every five years the Census Bureau counts every business in America. In 2022 it counted thirty-three thousand companies running nail salons. The four largest together took less than half of one percent of the sales. It counted under eight hundred companies running home centers, the giant hardware and building-supply stores. The four largest took ninety-eight percent. That share, the four largest firms' slice of an industry's sales, is called the four-firm concentration ratio.

Do that for all 897 industries the Census reports, and you get this. Most American industries are not very concentrated: in the median industry the four largest firms hold about 31 percent of sales, and in more than a quarter of industries they hold less than twenty. The long tail on the right is the castles: warehouse clubs, wireless carriers, tobacco, breakfast cereal, web search, kidney dialysis, where four firms or fewer hold most of the market. A warning before using these numbers. A market is where buyers can actually choose between sellers, and that is often smaller than a national industry: a town's only hospital is a monopoly whatever the national figure says. Antitrust lawyers spend careers arguing about exactly where a market's edges are.

The four-firm ratio ignores how the share is split. Regulators use a second measure, named after the economists Orris Herfindahl and Albert Hirschman. Square each firm's share of the market, in percent, and add them up. Four equal firms with a quarter each give two thousand five hundred. If one of them has fifty-five percent and the others fifteen each, the total jumps to nearly four thousand, because squaring makes the big firm count for much more. Twenty equal firms give five hundred. American competition authorities treat a market above one thousand eight hundred as highly concentrated, and look hard at any merger that pushes it there, or adds more than a hundred points to a market already above it.

Here is why regulators prefer the second measure. A market has four firms, with forty, thirty, twenty and ten percent. The four-firm ratio is a hundred percent; the HHI is three thousand. Now the two smallest merge. The four-firm ratio does not move: still a hundred percent. The HHI jumps by four hundred, to three thousand four hundred. Under the 2023 guidelines, a merger that leaves a market above eighteen hundred and adds more than a hundred points is presumed to lessen competition, and the companies have to show why it would not.
Walls: Chapter eight. Walls of cost and habit.

The first walls are made of cost. Part 4 showed that cost per unit falls with size and with experience. That is a moat. The incumbent sits at the bottom of the curve. A newcomer has to start small, at the top, and sell at the incumbent's price while its own costs are far higher. Warehouse clubs and supercenters are a case: the four largest companies had 96 percent of the industry's sales in 2022. To match their prices, a rival would need their buying power and their full stores from its first day. Sunk costs make the wall higher. A newcomer must risk money it cannot get back if it fails, while the incumbent spent the same money years ago, as Part 4's chapter on sunk costs showed.

The second walls are made of habit. A customer can walk across to a rival whenever she likes. But walking across costs something. Moving a bank account means new cards and new direct debits; moving a company to new software means retraining everyone; trying an unknown brand means a risk that the trusted one does not carry. The rival has to beat the incumbent by more than that toll before anyone moves. Brands are habit built up over decades. Industries that live on brands, soft drinks, household products, tobacco, earn some of the highest returns in Damodaran's table. And that is what Buffett said See's had: a durable advantage, built by the See's family over fifty years, that no rival could buy in a hurry.
Tobacco: Chapter nine. A moat that held.

Habit can hold a moat in place even while the market shrinks under it. In 1965, about 42 of every hundred American adults smoked cigarettes. By 2022, by the government's count, it was under 12. Few industries have lost customers so steadily for so long. And yet tobacco has earned the highest return on capital in Damodaran's table in seven of the last eleven years, and the second highest in the other four: between 45 and 96 percent since 2015. Every force is on its side. A few firms that rarely fight on price. Brands that smokers stay loyal to. Limits on advertising that keep newcomers from building a brand of their own. And a product that is, quite literally, a habit. With fewer customers every year, the castle has stayed full.
Networks: Chapter ten. Walls of networks and law.

The third kind of wall gets higher the more customers come. A network of two users has one connection. Add users one at a time, and the possible connections grow much faster than the users: twelve users, sixty-six connections. Each newcomer is worth more to join the big network than the small one, so the big one gets bigger. A payment card works this way twice over. Shoppers want the card that every shop takes; shops take the card that every shopper carries. Visa does not lend money or issue the cards: it runs the network between banks, shops and shoppers. In fiscal 2026 it turned 46 billion dollars of revenue into 28 billion of operating profit: 61 cents of every dollar. A rival with a better card would still have to sign up millions of shops and shoppers, each of whom wants the other to come first. Markets like this tend to tip: once one network is ahead, the gap feeds itself, and the second network shrinks rather than catches up. That is why so many of them end with one or two winners, and why their owners will spend heavily to be first.

A network can hold more than one castle. Visa has a rival with the same kind of network: Mastercard. The two compete for the same shops and the same shoppers. You might expect them to fight each other down to thin margins. They have not. Here is the share of each dollar of sales that Visa keeps as operating profit, every year since 2009, and here is Mastercard's: 58 cents in 2025. Two firms, side by side, both earning more than half of what they take in. Remember the two conditions from chapter seven: something keeps newcomers out, and the few do not fight. Here the network keeps newcomers out, since a new card is useless until shops take it, and shops will not take it until shoppers carry it. And the fees land mostly on shops, which cannot easily refuse the cards their customers carry, so the two have little reason to fight over them.

The fourth kind of wall is built by law. A patent gives an inventor the sole right to an invention for twenty years from the day the application is filed. Inside that wall the price can sit far above the cost of one more, which is how a new medicine can sell for many times what a pill costs to make. But this wall has a date on it. When the patent runs out, copies arrive, and the price falls towards the cost of making them. Licences and rights to scarce things work the same way without the expiry date: a broadcast licence, a bank charter, a slot to land at a crowded airport, a slice of the radio spectrum. Whoever holds one holds a piece of a market that others are not allowed to enter.
Forces: A moat keeps out one kind of attacker: newcomers. But a castle's treasure can leak away in other directions too. In 1979 Michael Porter, a young professor at Harvard Business School, drew the picture that business schools still teach. An industry's profit, he argued, is squeezed by five forces. The rivalry among the firms already inside. The threat of new entrants. The threat of substitutes, other ways of meeting the same need. The power of buyers to push prices down. And the power of suppliers to push costs up. Every one of them can drain the treasure, and the industries with lasting returns are those where all five are weak.

Hold two industries up to it. Airlines face all five at full strength. Their rivals cut fares to fill empty seats, as Part 4 showed. New airlines keep starting, because planes can be leased. Trains, cars and video calls are substitutes. Travellers compare every fare in seconds. And the suppliers are strong: two companies make almost every large airliner, and crews are unionized. Tobacco faces almost none of them. A few firms that rarely fight on price; brands and advertising limits that lock the leaders in; few substitutes; loyal customers; and a leaf bought from many farmers. Airlines earned 8 percent on their capital in 2025, by Damodaran's count; tobacco 63. Buffett's Kitty Hawk joke and Porter's diagram are saying the same thing.
Power: Two of Porter's forces are other companies: the customers who buy from an industry and the suppliers who sell to it. Part 1 of this series met them inside a phone. Apple buys its processors from TSMC, and its assembly from Foxconn. Both are giants. Both sell to the same customer. TSMC is the only company that can make Apple's processors at the scale and precision Apple needs. It keeps 62 cents of each dollar of sales after the direct cost of making them. Foxconn assembles phones, and Apple could move that work to Luxshare, Pegatron or Tata. Foxconn keeps 6 cents. Apple, the buyer, keeps 37 cents on its products. And Qualcomm, whose patents every phone maker must license, keeps 72 cents of its licensing revenue before tax. Same chain, same phones: the companies that cannot be replaced keep the money, and the ones that can be replaced work for a sliver. Buyer power is a moat drained by your own customer.
Steady: Chapter thirteen. A moat in the accounts.

What does a moat look like in a company's own accounts? Not, as you might think, a high margin. Here is the operating profit Visa kept from each dollar of sales, every year since 2009. Apart from one year with a large legal charge, it has stayed between about half and two thirds. Here is Costco. It keeps less than four cents of each dollar, a margin most businesses would call a disaster. But look at the line: it has hardly moved in seventeen years, and it has edged up. Buffett named Costco, with GEICO, as the kind of low-cost producer that has a moat: its prices are so low that a rival cannot undercut them. And here is Delta: a healthy margin in good years, then minus seventy-three percent in 2020. Measure how far each line wanders, and Costco's moves by less than half a point a year, Visa's by about 10, Delta's by 20. A moat shows up as a margin that rivals and recessions cannot push around, whatever its height.

Put every company in this series' filings on one chart. Along the bottom, each company's average operating margin since 2009. Up the side, how far that margin wanders from year to year. The steady ones sit along the bottom, at every height: Costco and Walmart with thin margins, NextEra and Microsoft in the middle, Mastercard and Visa at the top; Visa sits a little higher only because of its one-time legal charge in 2012. The wanderers sit above: Delta, Intel and Micron, whose margins swing with fuel, with chip prices and with the cycle that Part 6 is about. The height of a margin and its steadiness are different things. A moat shows up in the second.
Drained: Moats do not last for ever. The cleanest example is the newspaper. For most of a century a city's daily paper was one of the best businesses in America. It owned the printing press and the delivery vans, and it was the only place a shop could reach the whole town, or a family could sell a car or find a flat. In 2005 American newspapers took in an estimated 49 billion dollars from advertising, and about eleven billion from readers. By 2008, advertising was down to thirty-eight billion; by 2010, twenty-six. Then the classified ads moved to free websites, the shoppers' ads moved to search and social media, and the paper's moat, being the only way to reach the town, was simply walked round. By 2020, by Pew's estimate, advertising had fallen to about 9.6 billion, and readers were paying more than advertisers. No rival built a better newspaper. The thing the moat protected stopped being needed.

The same thing happened to photographic film. For a century Eastman Kodak sold the film, the chemicals and the paper, and a great deal of the profit came from the film itself, used once and bought again. Then photographs went digital, and then into the phone. In 2008 Kodak still sold 9.4 billion dollars' worth of goods. In January 2012 it filed for bankruptcy. By 2017 its sales were 1.5 billion. A moat protects a castle against rivals who want what is inside. It does nothing when the world stops wanting it. Part 6 is about how industries move through booms and busts; this series comes back to disruption in its later acts.
Called: Every part ends by scoring forecasts. This one has Buffett's. In 2008 he wrote that a durable advantage had proven elusive in airlines ever since the Wright brothers. Then the American airlines merged into a few big ones, and for a few years they earned well: fourteen to nineteen percent on their capital from 2015 to 2019, more than twice what it cost. Then came the pandemic, and two years of heavy losses. Since then, about eight percent. Across the eleven years, airlines earned 6.5 percent a year on their capital, against a cost of 6.0: hardly more than the capital could have earned anywhere else. Fewer, bigger airlines helped for a while; the five forces did the rest. Buffett called it.

And this part's own call, built on how sticky those returns have been. At least seven of the ten American industries with the highest return on capital in 2025 will still be among the twenty highest in 2028. Here is the top ten: tobacco, computers, general insurance, home centers, household products and the rest. In Damodaran's tables since 2015, seven or more of a year's top ten were still in the top twenty three years later in seven of eight cases. The one miss started in 2022, when a commodity boom briefly lifted steel, paper, coal and oil into the top ten; none of them had a moat, and all four fell back. We put it at seventy-five percent, a little below that record, because the record is short and the next shock is never the last one. It will be scored on his table for 2028, published in January 2029.
